newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Bosnia peace smashed Albanian pyramids - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia peace smashed Albanian pyramids - analysts.

text.p: The end of the civil war in the former Yugoslavia spelt doom for Albania's get-rich-quick investment schemes, which had thrived off the bloody conflict, analysts and bankers said on Friday.

A string of so-called pyramid savings funds, which sprung up following the collapse of Communism in 1990, have caved in over the past two months owing an estimated $2.0 billion and bringing Albania to the brink of economic chaos.
Under the pyramid system, interest is paid to older investors with deposits taken from the new. In past experience such funds swiftly ran out of new customers and went bust.
"A pure pyramid could survive only 18 months at most. In Albania they went on for years because they were much more complex," said one financial consultant with close ties to four of the schemes.
"If the Bosnian war was still going on, we wouldn't be in this mess today," he added.

Economists estimate that this tiny Balkan state made more than $1.0 million a day supplying Serbia and Montenegro with oil, in breach of a United Nations embargo. Diplomatic sources say big arms shipments were also routed to Bosnia via Albania.
Much of the money wound up in the investment accounts and analysts believe Albania soon became a haven for all types of illegal trade as the the Mafia also moved in.
An intelligence source in Rome told Reuters this week that it was "quite evident" that Italian mobsters pumped money into the private, unregulated funds to clean their illegal earnings.
A banker in Tirana said the last major shipment of dirty money arrived at the start of 1997, with the Mafia paying $1.5 million to a fund which laundered $20 million.

"The dirty money is plunged into the pyramids and clean money sent out under the guise of bogus import deals," said the banker, who declined to be named. "It is easy to watch the money clear the system."

However the days of regular money laundering ended last year, with the Mafia worried by the growing international attention being focused on Albania and attracted to the even less-well regulated markets in Bosnia.

Oil money also dried up following the lifting of the U.N. Yugoslav embargo at the end of 1995, and the Albanian savings firms, starved of their usual supply of funds, started to depend more on straight pyramid systems.
Last summer they engaged in a ruinous interest rate war, offering absurd returns to draw custom and stay alive.

In the absence of an efficient banking system, most Albanians placed their savings in the pyramids over the past five years and increasingly came to depend on the interest to supplement their meagre wages.

The funds were advertised on state television and buildings owned by the schemes were guarded by policemen. Opposition parties allege that the ruling Democratic Party turned to the firms to help pay for its 1996 general election campaign.

Albanians certainly believed that the funds had an official stamp of approval and when interest rates were hiked, money poured in from Albania's army of illegal emigrants while many impoverished locals sold everything they had in the expectation of doubling their cash in a matter of weeks.
The International Monetary Fund sounded the alarm bells last October, prompting the government to issue its first warning about the danger of the funds.
"At that stage some of the pyramids decided to cut their loses and in December more money left Albania than entered for the first time in years," the financial consultant said.
Five national schemes have now gone officially bust.

Another four companies, which deny they are pyramids and say they are corporate holdings, are still clinging to life but they have all drastically cut back their interest payments and have frozen depositors' assets.
